after.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-5x+3?$
after.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

${x}^{3}$
${x}^{2}$
${x}^{1}$
${x}^{0}$ 

 
$1$
$1$
$1$
$-5$
$3$

 

$↓$
$1$
$2$
$-3$

 

$1$
$2$
$-3$
$0$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}+2x-3,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}+2x-3).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-1)(x+3)(x-1) \\  & =(x+3)(x-1{)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $2.$

after.worked_solution:
Since $x=4$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

${x}^{2}$

${x}^{0}$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-4}={x}^{2}-3x+2,

which means

p(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}-3x+2).

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-4)(x-1)(x-2).\end{aligned}
